segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He also came to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman but of a Greek father,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who was well spoken of by the brothers and sisters in Lystra and Iconium.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul wanted this man to go out with him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they traveled through the cities, they handed on to them the decrees decided on by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, to be kept.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the assemblies were being strengthened in the faith and were growing in number day by day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They went through the Phrygian and Galatian region, having been prevented by the Holy Spirit from speaking the word in Asia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they came up to Mysia, they tried to go on into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not let them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And a vision appeared to Paul during the night: a Macedonian man was standing there, appealing to him and saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Cross over to Macedonia and help us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had seen the vision, we immediately sought to go on to Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to bring the good news to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So, putting out to sea from Troas, we ran a straight course to Samothrace, and on the next day to Neapolis,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of that district of Macedonia, a colony. We stayed in this city for some days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to a riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had gathered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A woman named Lydia was listening, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira who worshiped God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what Paul was saying.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When she and her household had been baptized, she appealed to us, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And she prevailed on us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It happened that, as we were going to the place of prayer, a slave girl who had a spirit of divination met us; she brought her owners a great deal of profit by fortune-telling.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She followed Paul and us, crying out,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “These men are slaves of the Most High God, who are proclaiming to you a way of salvation.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She kept doing this for many days. But Paul, exasperated, turned and said to the spirit,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it came out that very hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when her owners saw that their hope of profit had gone out, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the authorities,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and bringing them to the magistrates they said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “These men are throwing our city into turmoil. They are Jews,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and they are proclaiming customs that it is not lawful for us, being Romans, to accept or practice.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The crowd joined in the attack against them, and the magistrates tore the clothes off them and ordered them to be beaten with rods.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After inflicting many blows on them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to guard them securely.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having received such an order, he threw them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; at once all the doors were opened, and everyone’s chains came loose.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The jailer woke up, and when he saw the doors of the prison open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Paul called out in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do yourself no harm, for we are all here!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He called for lights and rushed in, and trembling he fell down before Paul and Silas.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he brought them outside and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they spoke the word of the Lord to him, together with all who were in his house.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that hour of the night he took them and washed their wounds, and at once he was baptized, he and all who belonged to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he brought them up into his house and set a meal before them, and he rejoiced with his whole household, having come to believe in God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When day came, the magistrates sent the lictors, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Release those men.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The jailer reported these words to Paul:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The magistrates have sent word that you are to be released. So now come out and go in peace.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Paul said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “They beat us in public without trial, men who are Romans, and threw us into prison, and now they are throwing us out in secret? No indeed! Let them come themselves and lead us out.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The lictors reported these words to the magistrates, who were afraid when they heard that they were Romans.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they came and appealed to them, and when they had led them out they asked them to leave the city.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After leaving the prison they went to Lydia’s house; and when they had seen the brothers and sisters, they encouraged them and departed.

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address or describe a mixed group of men and women, and here it means the members of the community in general. In verse 40 the group meets in Lydia’s house and plainly includes her. Older translations have “brethren” or “brothers”; many recent ones render it as here.

The Greek word meant a gathering of people, used both for a city’s civic assembly and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel gathered before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

notes.traditional: the region of Phrygia and Galatia
notes.note: The Greek can mean one region that was both Phrygian and Galatian (the part of Phrygia inside the Roman province of Galatia) or two regions, Phrygia and then the Galatian territory further north. The choice bears on the long-running debate over which communities Paul’s letter to the Galatians was written to. Scholars remain divided.
This is the Roman province of Asia, the western part of modern Turkey with Ephesus as its chief city, not the continent.

Here the narrative shifts without explanation from “they” to “we”, the first of several such passages in Acts. The traditional and still common view is that the author was a companion of Paul who joined the party at Troas. Others think he is drawing on a travel diary or using a literary convention.

notes.phrase: a leading city of that district of Macedonia
notes.traditional: the chief city of that part of Macedonia
notes.note: The manuscripts vary here, and the best-attested wording is awkward: literally “first city of the district of Macedonia”. Roman Macedonia was divided into four districts. Philippi lay in the first, but Amphipolis was that district’s capital and Thessalonica the provincial capital. Some editors therefore adopt a slightly different reading, “a city of the first district of Macedonia”; the rendering here follows the SBLGNT text and takes “first” as “leading”.

Luke uses the Latin word. A Roman colony was a city settled largely by army veterans, governed by Roman law with its own Roman-style magistrates, and its citizens held Roman citizenship. This explains the pride in being “Romans” in verse 21 and the officials named in the rest of the chapter.

The word ordinarily means “prayer”, but Jewish communities also used it for their meeting place, sometimes a building and sometimes an open-air spot near water. Whether Philippi had a synagogue building is unknown; that only women are mentioned may suggest a small community. Some manuscripts read instead “where prayer was customarily made”.

In Acts this expression describes Gentiles who were attached to the synagogue and worshiped Israel’s God without having become full converts to Judaism. Lydia is thus presented as a non-Jew who already revered the God of the Jews.

The Greek is literally “a spirit, a python”. Python was the serpent of Delphi in Greek myth, slain by Apollo, whose oracle there was the most famous in the Greek world. By this period the word was used of soothsayers believed to have a spirit speaking through them. A first-century reader would have heard an association with pagan oracles that the English phrase does not carry.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and the speaker is herself a slave with owners. “Servants” is the traditional rendering and avoids the associations of modern slavery, but it suggests a hired employee, which the word did not mean.

The Greek has no article, so it may be “a way” or “the way” of salvation; most translations have “the way”. “Most High God” was used by Jews for the God of Israel, but pagans also used it for Zeus or another supreme deity. In a pagan city the girl’s cry could therefore be heard as announcing one path of deliverance from one high god among others, which may be part of why Paul silenced it.

The Greek title was the usual equivalent of the Latin “praetor”. A Roman colony was headed by a pair of chief magistrates, and Luke gives them the Greek title commonly used for such officials. They had authority to hear charges and order punishment.

The jailer’s respectful address is the plural of the word translated “Lord” in the reply that follows, and “owners” in verses 16 and 19. The answer in verse 31 picks the word up and points him from these “lords” to the Lord Jesus.

The Greek word, literally “rod-carrier”, was the standard term for Roman lictors, the attendants who walked before magistrates carrying bundles of rods and who carried out their orders, including beatings. It shares its root with “beaten with rods” in verse 22. “Police” suggests a modern institution that did not exist.

“Romans” here means holders of Roman citizenship. Roman law protected citizens from being beaten or imprisoned without a proper trial, and officials who violated this could face serious consequences, hence the magistrates’ fear in verse 38. There is irony in the echo of verse 21, where the accusers had appealed to their own standing as Romans.

candidates.reason: The plural for community members occurs throughout Acts and the letters, and translators split between “brothers”, “brothers and sisters” and “believers”; the choice should be uniform.
“Slave” versus “servant” is a pervasive and contested choice across the Gospels, Acts and the letters, and it was not in the register entries supplied for this chapter.
The verb ranges over urge, appeal, comfort and encourage across the whole New Testament, and a fixed rendering per sense would prevent drift between chapters.
It recurs constantly in Luke–Acts and Paul, and varies in English between “preach the gospel”, “proclaim the good news” and “evangelize”; it should match whatever is decided for εὐαγγέλιον.
It is used for Jewish and Christian leaders across many books, where “elders”, “presbyters” and “older men” are all possible and readers would be misled by variation.
